catalog_quote: Kung is a tone language and exhibits three level tones (high, mid and low), and three contour tones (rising, high-mid and falling).Worth mentioning is the fact that Kung is a register tone language and as such, realizations of contour tones are a result of a combination of register tones. Yip (2002: 1) states that, “a language is a ‘tone language’ if the pitch of the word can change the meaning of the word. Not just its nuances, but its core meaning.”The following data show contrast between the three underlying tones. (3) H mbáŋ ‘salt’ L mbàŋ ‘stick’ ... kú ‘die’ kù ‘defecate’ ... [p. 25, §2.5] Kung exhibits the V, CV, CGV, CVC and CGVC syllable structures, where G stands for ‘glide’. Words in the language consist mostly of monosyllabic roots with a possible V- or CV- prefix or suffix.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand description states that Kung is a register tone language with three underlying level tones (H, M, L) and derived contour tones; it makes no statement at all about word stress or accent. No source examined says where stress falls or whether stress exists.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source is silent on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statement is about lexical (word-level) tone on citation forms; §2.5 (p. 25) adds that words 'consist mostly of monosyllabic roots with a possible V- or CV- prefix or suffix', so a word-stress rule would in any case be near-trivial for most of the lexicon.
new_statements.identity_note: Tatang 2016 describes the Kung of Kung village, Fungom subdivision (Lower Fungom), data from three named elders; this is the single variety behind kung1260 (Glottolog alt name Cungo). Wikipedia's 'Nzonko/Nkam/Zoro dialect' lines are unsupported by any source opened. Not to be confused with ǃKung (Kxʼa, southern Africa).

sources.note: Chapter 2 Phonology (consonants, vowels, §2.4 Tones p.23, §2.5 syllable structure pp.25-27, §2.6 processes): 'Kung is a tone language' with three level tones (H, M, L) and three contour tones (rising, high-mid, falling), analysed as a register-tone language whose contours are combinations of level tones. Words are mostly monosyllabic roots with V-/CV- prefixes. The words stress/accent/prominence/intonation/suprasegmental do not occur anywhere in the thesis (0 a full-text search for stress/accent hits in full-text extraction).
Phonology section (consonants, vowels, six tones) is drawn entirely from Tatang 2016; supplied the open URL of the thesis on Jeff Good's site. Nothing on stress.
